## Abstract


The influence of 6-phosphofructo-1-kinase on glycolytic flux in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae was assessed by measuring the effects of enzyme overexpression on glucose consumption, ethanol production, and glycolytic intermediate levels under aerobic and anaerobic conditions. Enzyme overexpression had no effect on glycolytic flux under anaerobic conditions, but under aerobic conditions, it

chunk:2:range:3983:7893:part:800.text: increased glycolytic flux up to the anaerobic level. The Pasteur effect was thus abolished in these cells. The increased glycolytic flux was accompanied by a compensatory decrease in flux in oxidative phosphorylation. The concentrations of the enzyme substrates showed only small or insignificant changes. These data imply that the enzyme has a low flux control coefficient for glycolysis. However, in cells overexpressing the enzyme, there was a compensatory decrease in 6-phosphofructo-2-kinase activity which was accompanied by a corresponding decrease in fructose 2,6-bisphosphate concentration. findings.finding: The abstract opens: “The influence of 6-phosphofructo-1-kinase on glycolytic flux in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae was assessed by measuring the effects of enzyme overexpression on glucose consumption, ethanol production, and glycolytic intermediate levels under aerobic and anaerobic conditions.” This identifies the intervention and measured endpoints, but gives neither the magnitude nor the construction of overexpression.

Reported experimental outcomes, abstract sentences 2–5: “Enzyme overexpression had no effect on glycolytic flux under anaerobic conditions, but under aerobic conditions, it increased glycolytic flux up to the anaerobic level. The Pasteur effect was thus abolished in these cells. The increased glycolytic flux was accompanied by a compensatory decrease in flux in oxidative phosphorylation. The concentrations of the enzyme substrates showed only small or insignificant changes.” Sentence 2 starts in part:0 and ends in part:800. These are qualitative results, not numerical glucose-consumption or ethanol-production rates. The term “compensatory” is the authors’ interpretation of the accompanying oxidative-phosphorylation change.

findings.finding: The abstract distinguishes an inference about control from accompanying measurements: “These data imply that the enzyme has a low flux control coefficient for glycolysis. However, in cells overexpressing the enzyme, there was a compensatory decrease in 6-phosphofructo-2-kinase activity which was accompanied by a corresponding decrease in fructose 2,6-bisphosphate concentration.” The low control coefficient is an interpretation, not a reported numerical coefficient. Decreased 6-phosphofructo-2-kinase activity and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate concentration are reported qualitative experimental outcomes; their characterization as compensatory is interpretive.

reading_memory.summary: PubMed record 1533788 now supplies the complete Davies and Brindle abstract across chunk:2:range:3983:7893:part:0, part:800 and the opening of part:1600. It describes 6-phosphofructo-1-kinase overexpression in Saccharomyces cerevisiae with glucose consumption, ethanol production and glycolytic intermediates assessed aerobically and anaerobically. Reported qualitative results: no anaerobic glycolytic-flux effect; aerobic flux increased to the anaerobic level, abolishing the Pasteur effect; accompanying decreased oxidative-phosphorylation flux; small or insignificant substrate-concentration changes; decreased 6-phosphofructo-2-kinase activity and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate concentration. Low flux control coefficient is an inference. In-vitro measurements support the possibility that reduced fructose 2,6-bisphosphate lowers specific activity in the cell enough to compensate for increased enzyme concentration; this is not a numerical in-vivo compensation measurement. No numerical rates, activities, concentrations, overexpression magnitude, units, uncertainties, sample sizes, construction details, steady-state declaration or rate equations are supplied. The Full text links heading has no exposed target URL.
